item.title: Bungo Beef: Oita's Premium Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Bungo beef (Bungo-gyu), named after Oita’s historic Bungo province, is the prefecture’s premium brand of wagyu and a source of great local pride. Reared to strict standards on Oita’s rich natural pastures and pure water, the black-haired cattle produce beef renowned for its exquisite fine marbling, tenderness and deep, sweet flavour, ranking it among Japan’s fine regional wagyu. The low-melting-point fat gives it a rich, buttery texture that melts in the mouth.

item.title: Miyazaki Beef: Champion Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Miyazaki beef (Miyazaki-gyu) is one of Japan’s most acclaimed brands of wagyu — famously crowned the nation’s best at the prestigious ‘Wagyu Olympics’ national competition multiple times, a source of enormous local pride. Raised to strict standards from black-haired Japanese cattle in Miyazaki’s warm, green countryside, this premium beef is renowned for its exquisite fine marbling, deep umami flavour and remarkable tenderness. The fat melts at a low temperature, giving a rich, buttery, melt-in-the-mouth texture and a sweet, lingering taste that ranks it among the very finest beef in the country.

item.title: Saga Beef: A Premium Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Saga beef (Saga-gyu) is one of Japan’s most prized brands of wagyu, a premium black-haired Japanese beef raised to strict standards in the prefecture. It is renowned for its exquisite marbling — fine ribbons of fat woven through deep-red meat — which melts at a low temperature to give an intensely rich, buttery, tender mouthfeel and a sweet, deep flavour, ranking it among the finest beef in the country. In Saga city and across the prefecture, restaurants serve it in every classic style: seared as steak or teppanyaki, dipped in sukiyaki or shabu-shabu hotpot, grilled as yakiniku, or in a beef bowl or hamburger steak for a more casual taste.

item.title: Tottori Wagyu Beef: The Original Champion Bloodline — Guide
item.description: Tottori has an outsized place in the story of Japanese beef: the prefecture’s cattle descend in large part from a legendary stud bull, Ketaka-go, whose bloodline was so prized that it underpins many of Japan’s most famous wagyu brands elsewhere. Yet Tottori beef is far less known than the names it helped create, which makes it something of an insider’s choice. The local wagyu is specifically prized for its high oleic-acid content — a fat that melts at low temperature and gives a clean, sweet richness — and is served in the city and at farms as steak, sukiyaki, shabu-shabu and yakiniku, often at gentler prices than the headline brands.

item.title: Yamagata Beef: Clean, Sweet Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Yamagata beef (Yamagata Gyu) is one of Japan’s certified branded wagyu strains — raised on the clean mountain water and feed of the Shonai and Okitama regions, the cattle develop exceptional marbling and a distinctively clean, sweet fat that distinguishes it from Kobe or Matsusaka styles. Look for it as shabu-shabu, sukiyaki or grilled thinly over charcoal at specialist restaurants in Yamagata City. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Yamagata City & beyond Hours Restaurant hours Admission Premium; varies by cut Time needed About 1.

item.title: Best Wagyu Beef in Japan Where to Eat Guide
item.description: Best Wagyu Beef in Japan: Where to Eat Guide for the Ultimate Beef Experience There is no food experience on Earth quite like eating authentic wagyu beef in Japan. If you’ve come across this best wagyu beef in Japan where to eat guide, you’re already on the right track — but let me be honest with you: after fifteen years of living here, exploring every corner of this country, and eating more wagyu than my doctor would probably approve of, I can tell you that what most tourists experience as “wagyu” barely scratches the surface.
